title: Reconciling GW170817 and GW190814 with a Nonmonotonic Sound-Speed Equation of State
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
summary: We show that the GW170817-GW190814 tension can be reconciled within General Relativity by a structured causal EoS basin found with a Constrained Evolutionary TOV Discovery pipeline (CETD). The basin contains ~1.4x10^4 unique EoS with M_max = 2.3-2.8 M_sun, R_1.4 = 11.97-12.29 km, Lambda_1.4 <= 580, and double-peaked sound speeds reaching c_s^2/c^2 = 0.86-0.99.

AI.tldr: The GW170817-GW190814 tension in neutron star masses can be resolved within General Relativity using a novel CETD pipeline, which identifies a structured basin of ~14,000 causal equations of state with specific mass, radius, tidal deformability, and sound speed ranges.
AI.motivation: To reconcile the apparent tension between gravitational wave events GW170817 (binary neutron star merger) and GW190814 (which involved a ~2.5-2.6 M_sun compact object) within the framework of General Relativity, without invoking exotic physics.
AI.method: A Constrained Evolutionary TOV Discovery pipeline (CETD) was developed to systematically explore the space of causal equations of state (EoS) under the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, identifying a structured EoS basin that satisfies constraints from both events.
AI.result: Found ~1.4×10^4 unique EoS with maximum masses 2.3-2.8 M_sun, radii at 1.4 M_sun of 11.97-12.29 km, tidal deformability at 1.4 M_sun ≤ 580, and double-peaked sound speeds reaching 0.86-0.99c^2.
AI.conclusion: The GW170817-GW190814 tension can be resolved within standard General Relativity through appropriate causal EoS modeling, without requiring modifications to gravity or exotic matter.

title: Magnetic Eruption and Nucleosynthesis in GRνMHD Simulations of Spinning Neutron Star Mergers
comment: 21 pages, 25 figures, REVTeX 4.2
summary: We present three-dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations of equal-mass binary neutron star mergers with varied neutron star spin configurations and second-moment neutrino transport, following the formation and early evolution of long-lived remnants. We compare a fiducial irrotational binary with binaries having spins that are aligned or antialigned with the orbital angular momentum, and examime how spin affects the merger dynamics, magnetic field evolution, outflows, and nucleosynthesis. Compared to the fiducial case, the aligned spin configuration releases more cold, neutron-rich tidal ejecta in the equatorial plane, which enables the development of a more tightly collimated polar outflow erupting from the remnant and inner accretion disk. Conversely, the case with spins antialigned with the orbit experiences a more violent collision at merger, disrupting magnetic amplification, loading the environment with debris, and impeding the propagation of magnetically driven winds. Strong neutrino reprocessing of the polar outflow in the irrotational and aligned spin cases produces $2.4\times 10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ of proton-rich ($Y_e \geq 0.49$) material, resulting in the synthesis of light r-process elements including $^{56}Ni$, whose subsequent decay potentially sends a unique electromagnetic signal from long-lived remnants. However, the outflows remain too dense and slow to be consistent with typical short gamma-ray bursts.

AI.tldr: 3D GRMHD simulations of binary neutron star mergers with varied spin configurations show that aligned spins produce more collimated polar outflows and proton-rich ejecta ($2.4\times10^{-3} M_\odot$ of $Y_e\geq0.49$ material including $^{56}$Ni), while antialigned spins disrupt magnetic amplification and outflows; none produce typical short GRB outflows.
AI.motivation: To understand how neutron star spin configurations affect merger dynamics, magnetic field evolution, outflows, and nucleosynthesis in binary neutron star mergers that produce long-lived remnants.
AI.method: 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations with second-moment neutrino transport, comparing irrotational, aligned-spin, and antialigned-spin equal-mass binary neutron star mergers.
AI.result: Aligned spins produce more cold neutron-rich tidal ejecta and tighter collimated polar outflows; antialigned spins cause violent collisions that disrupt magnetic amplification. The irrotational and aligned cases yield $2.4\times 10^{-3} M_\odot$ of proton-rich ($Y_e\geq0.49$) ejecta, synthesizing light r-process elements including $^{56}$Ni. Outflows are too dense and slow for typical short GRBs.
AI.conclusion: Neutron star spin orientation significantly impacts merger dynamics and nucleosynthetic yields; proton-rich outflows from long-lived remnants produce $^{56}$Ni whose decay could yield a unique electromagnetic signal, but these outflows are inconsistent with typical short gamma-ray burst properties.

title: Interstellar Scintillation of Three Nearby Pulsars with FAST
comment: Journal of High Energy Astrophysics (JHEAp), doi:10.1016/j.jheap.2026.100628
summary: Interstellar scintillation probes the properties of the ionized interstellar medium as well as the dynamical behavior of pulsars themselves. Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope, we obtained hour-long observations of PSRs~J0837+0610, J1136+1551, and J1239+2453. We detected a single scintillation arc in PSRs~J0837+0610 and J1239+2453, and identified three distinct arcs in PSR~J1136+1551. Our analysis reveals that the arc curvature scales with observing frequency as $η\propto ν^{-2.0\pm0.6}$ for PSR J0837+0610, and as $η\propto ν^{-1.9\pm0.6}$ for PSR J1239+2453. For PSR J1136+1551, the two clearest arcs exhibit scaling relations of $η\propto ν^{-1.6\pm0.6}$ and $η\propto ν^{-2.0\pm0.4}$, respectively. However, the frequency dependence of the third arc could not be constrained due to its low signal-to-noise ratio at higher frequencies. Moreover, the corresponding scattering screens are measured at distances ranging from 30 to 420 pc from Earth. However, long-term scintillation monitoring or VLBI observations are needed to reliably measure the scattering screen.

AI.tldr: Using FAST telescope observations of three pulsars (J0837+0610, J1136+1551, J1239+2453), we detected scintillation arcs and measured their curvature scaling with frequency ($\eta \propto \nu^{-1.6}$ to $\nu^{-2.0}$). Scattering screen distances range from 30–420 pc, though long-term monitoring or VLBI is needed for reliable measurements.
AI.motivation: To probe the properties of the ionized interstellar medium and pulsar dynamics through interstellar scintillation analysis using high-sensitivity FAST observations.
AI.method: Hour-long FAST observations of three pulsars; detection and analysis of scintillation arcs; measurement of arc curvature frequency scaling relations; estimation of scattering screen distances.
AI.result:
Single scintillation arc in J0837+0610 and J1239+2453; three arcs in J1136+1551. Curvature scaling: $\eta \propto 
u^{-2.0\pm0.6}$ (J0837+0610), $\eta \propto 
u^{-1.9\pm0.6}$ (J1239+2453), and $\eta \propto 
u^{-1.6\pm0.6}$ and $\eta \propto 
u^{-2.0\pm0.4}$ for two arcs in J1136+1551. Third arc unconstrained. Scattering screen distances: 30–420 pc.
AI.conclusion: Scintillation arcs and frequency-dependent curvature are successfully measured for three pulsars, but long-term monitoring or VLBI is required for reliable scattering screen distance measurements.

title: The MeerKAT Thousand-Pulsar Polarisation Array II: Searches for Ultralight Axion-Like Dark Matter
comment: 14 pages in total, 9 figures
summary: We construct Pulsar Polarisation Arrays (PPA), using regular pulsars monitored in MeerKAT's Thousand Pulsar Array (TPA) Programme, to search for Axion-like Dark Matter (ALDM) within Milky Way. Specifically, from a catalogue of 1237 regular pulsars, we select the 50 ones with the highest signal-to-noise ratio and set upper limits on the ALDM Chern-Simons coupling. We find no signals with statistical significance over the mass range of $[10^{-23},10^{-20}]\,{\rm eV}$ in the six-year MeerKAT's data. By combining the high-quality TPA pulsars and the accurate ionospheric subtraction of spinifex, we establish the most sensitive upper limits to the date on the ALDM Chern-Simons coupling, namely $\lesssim 10^{-14} - 3\times 10^{-13}\,{\rm GeV}^{-1}$, for the mass range of $[10^{-23},10^{-21}]\,{\rm eV}$ except at $m_a \sim 1.3 \times 10^{-22}\,$eV. This study underscores the great potential of constructing regular-pulsar PPAs for scientific tasks.

AI.tldr: Using 50 high-SNR pulsars from MeerKAT's Thousand Pulsar Array, the authors construct Pulsar Polarisation Arrays (PPA) to search for Axion-like Dark Matter (ALDM) via the Chern-Simons coupling. No significant signal is found over mass range [10⁻²³, 10⁻²⁰] eV in six years of data. They set the most sensitive upper limits to date, ~10⁻¹⁴–3×10⁻¹³ GeV⁻¹ for masses [10⁻²³, 10⁻²¹] eV (except at m_a ~ 1.3×10⁻²² eV), demonstrating the potential of regular-pulsar PPAs.
AI.motivation: To search for Axion-like Dark Matter (ALDM) using pulsar polarisation data, leveraging the large regular-pulsar catalogue from MeerKAT's Thousand Pulsar Array (TPA) Programme to set constraints on the ALDM Chern-Simons coupling.
AI.method: From a catalogue of 1237 regular pulsars, the 50 with highest signal-to-noise ratio are selected to construct a Pulsar Polarisation Array (PPA). Six-year MeerKAT data are used, with ionospheric subtraction performed via the spinifex pipeline. Upper limits on the ALDM Chern-Simons coupling are derived over the mass range [10⁻²³, 10⁻²⁰] eV.
AI.result: No statistically significant ALDM signals are detected. The most sensitive upper limits to date are established: ≲ 10⁻¹⁴–3×10⁻¹³ GeV⁻¹ for mass range [10⁻²³, 10⁻²¹] eV, with an exclusion gap at m_a ~ 1.3×10⁻²² eV.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that constructing Pulsar Polarisation Arrays from regular pulsars holds great potential for dark matter searches and other scientific tasks.

title: Observing the Peculiar Acceleration of our Solar System with Quasar Proper Motions
comment: 18 pages, 17 figures, 1 table, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We measure the proper motion dipole of quasars observed by Gaia to determine the acceleration of the Solar System with respect to the quasar rest frame. We characterise the full angular power spectrum of the proper motion field using the pseudo-$C_\ell$ formalism and employ simulation-based inference to jointly constrain the dipole and higher multipole power. Cross-correlation with the Gaia scanning strategy, stellar density, and stellar proper motion maps is used to diagnose the origin of systematic power beyond the dipole. We apply this framework to both the Gaia EDR3 quasar catalogue and the Quaia catalogue. The inferred acceleration is consistent with the previous determination, but the credible intervals widen by factors of 1.5 to 2.5 when higher-multipole degeneracies are properly marginalised, indicating that previous uncertainty estimates were optimistic. Our best estimate, based on the Quaia catalogue is $(g_x,\, g_y, \,g_z) =( 0.40^{+0.70}_{-0.70},\,-5.09^{+0.54}_{-0.54},\,-2.40^{+0.55}_{-0.58}) \;μas \,yr^{-1}$, corresponding to an amplitude of $5.72_{-0.52}^{+0.53}\,\rm μas\,yr^{-1}$. The acceleration shows no significant dependence on source redshift, providing further evidence for its kinematic origin.

AI.tldr: Using Gaia quasar proper motions and simulation-based inference, the authors measure the Solar System's acceleration dipole, finding consistency with previous results but with 1.5–2.5× wider credible intervals after marginalizing higher-multipole systematic power. Their Quaia-based estimate yields acceleration amplitude 5.72 μas yr⁻¹, with no significant redshift dependence.
AI.motivation: To determine the Solar System's acceleration with respect to the quasar rest frame by measuring the proper motion dipole of Gaia quasars, and to properly account for systematic errors beyond the dipole that may have been underestimated in prior work.
AI.method: Full angular power spectrum analysis using pseudo-Cℓ formalism, joint constraints on dipole and higher multipole power via simulation-based inference, cross-correlation with Gaia scanning strategy, stellar density, and stellar proper motion maps to diagnose systematics.
AI.result: Inferred acceleration consistent with previous determination, but credible intervals widen by factors 1.5–2.5 when higher-multipole degeneracies are properly marginalized. Best estimate from Quaia: (g_x, g_y, g_z) = (0.40⁺⁰·⁷⁰₋₀.₇₀, –5.09⁺⁰·⁵⁴₋₀.₅₄, –2.40⁺⁰·⁵⁵₋₀.₅₈) μas yr⁻¹, amplitude 5.72⁺⁰·⁵³₋₀.₅₂ μas yr⁻¹. No significant redshift dependence.
AI.conclusion: Previous uncertainty estimates for the Solar System acceleration from Gaia quasar proper motions were optimistic; properly marginalizing systematic multipoles yields larger uncertainties. The kinematic origin of the signal is supported by the absence of redshift dependence.

title: Extreme Transients in Gamma Rays
summary: Extreme gamma-ray transients represent some of the most energetic and physically constraining phenomena in high-energy astrophysics. They are characterized by rapid, large-amplitude variability and by physical conditions approaching fundamental limits on particle acceleration, cooling, and compactness. In this review, we focus on transients detected above around 100 MeV and define extreme events as either those involving catastrophic transformations of astrophysical systems (such as stellar explosions, compact-object mergers, and tidal-disruption events) or those exhibiting evidence for particle acceleration operating in an extreme regime. These systems are powered by the rapid release of gravitational, magnetic, nuclear, or kinetic energy, with shocks and magnetic reconnection playing a central role in producing ultra-relativistic particle populations and non-thermal radiation. We summarize observational and theoretical diagnostics that constrain the size, magnetization, and Lorentz factor of the emitting region, including variability timescales, luminosity-timescale correlations, and spectral evolution across the MeV-TeV domain. We further review the complementary capabilities of space-borne gamma-ray instruments, ground-based Cherenkov and air-shower observatories in detecting short-lived, high-energy outbursts. Extreme transient classes discussed include gamma-ray bursts, novae, rapidly variable emission from extragalactic and Galactic jets. Also, because of its extreme aspects, we include flaring emission detected from the Crab Nebula. While each type of these flares poses interesting challenges for phenomenology and theory of these sources, together, these events form the landscape of extreme gamma-ray variability.

AI.tldr: This review covers extreme gamma-ray transients (>100 MeV) from catastrophic astrophysical events (explosions, mergers, tidal disruptions) and extreme particle acceleration sources, summarizing observational/theoretical diagnostics of emitting regions, detection capabilities across instruments, and classes including GRBs, novae, jets, and Crab Nebula flares.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of extreme gamma-ray transients—the most energetic, rapidly varying phenomena in high-energy astrophysics—and to systematize the observational and theoretical diagnostics that constrain their physical conditions.
AI.method: Review of observational and theoretical diagnostics (variability timescales, luminosity-timescale correlations, spectral evolution) across MeV-TeV domain; comparison of detection capabilities of space-borne gamma-ray instruments, ground-based Cherenkov, and air-shower observatories.
AI.result: Identifies key extreme transient classes: gamma-ray bursts, novae, rapidly variable emission from jets, and Crab Nebula flares. Summarizes constraints on emitting-region size, magnetization, and Lorentz factor from variability and spectral data.
AI.conclusion: Extreme gamma-ray transients collectively form a landscape of extreme variability, with each class posing unique challenges for phenomenology and theory, while shocks and magnetic reconnection are central to powering ultra-relativistic particles and non-thermal emission.

title: High-redshift GRB 140304A at z = 5.282 with flaring activity: A multi-wavelength study
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. This article presents a detailed multi-wavelength analysis of GRB 140304A at z = 5.282, having uncommon late-time flaring features. The aim is to study GRB 140304A and other similar bursts to understand stellar evolution and formation processes at high-z. Aims. GRBs at high-z, possible flaring activities at different frequencies seen at relatively late-times, help to constrain temporal correlation among contemporaneous flares. In the present study, we plan to constrain such a temporal and spectral study for a sample of high-z bursts, including GRB 140304A. Methods. We use Swift, Fermi, and ground-based observations to constrain the temporal and spectral properties of the prompt and afterglow emissions. Using the cross-correlation function, we calculate the spectral lag in the light curves observed in two energy bands of Swift's Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) and X-ray Telescope (XRT). Results. Parameter evolution of the prompt emission analysis reveals a hard-to-soft evolution of the spectral peak energy (Ep) and the magnetic field strength (B), consistent with the typical population of long GRBs. For GRB 140304A, a rare pattern of spectral lag evolution having positive lag in the early BAT light curves, but no lag is observed in the XRT light curves. We have also observed systematic time delays among the peak times of flares in three different bands, but the optical flares exhibit a morphological correspondence with X-ray or gamma-ray flares. Conclusions. Our analysis shows that the observed positive spectral lag in GRB 140304A is closely related to the hard-to-soft spectral evolution during the prompt emission phase, as seen in some of the other long GRBs. Additionally, there is a clear connection between gamma-ray, X-ray and optical flares with prompt emission, which are produced through synchrotron radiation during rapid bulk acceleration within the emitting region.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes GRB 140304A at z=5.282, focusing on its uncommon late-time flaring features. Using Swift, Fermi, and ground-based observations, the authors find hard-to-soft spectral evolution with positive spectral lag in early BAT light curves but no lag in XRT. Optical flares show morphological correspondence with gamma-ray/X-ray flares, indicating a common synchrotron radiation origin during rapid bulk acceleration.
AI.motivation: To study GRB 140304A and similar high-z bursts to understand stellar evolution and formation processes at high redshift, particularly by constraining temporal correlations among contemporaneous flares observed at late times across different frequencies.
AI.method: The study uses Swift, Fermi, and ground-based observations to constrain temporal and spectral properties of prompt and afterglow emissions. Cross-correlation functions calculate spectral lags in light curves from Swift's BAT (two energy bands) and XRT. Parameter evolution of prompt emission is analyzed, and time delays among flare peaks in gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical bands are examined.
AI.result: Prompt emission analysis shows hard-to-soft evolution of spectral peak energy (Ep) and magnetic field strength (B), consistent with typical long GRBs. GRB 140304A exhibits a rare spectral lag pattern: positive lag in early BAT light curves but no lag in XRT. Systematic time delays are found among flare peaks in three bands, with optical flares showing morphological correspondence to X-ray/gamma-ray flares.
AI.conclusion: The positive spectral lag in GRB 140304A relates to hard-to-soft spectral evolution during prompt emission, similar to other long GRBs. A clear connection exists between gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical flares and prompt emission, all produced via synchrotron radiation during rapid bulk acceleration within the emitting region.

title: Neutron Star Equation of State via Physics Informed Neural Network
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures
summary: We present the first application, to the best of our knowledge, of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to the neutron star equation-of-state (EOS) inverse problem. Two interacting networks -- one representing the EOS $P(\varepsilon)$ as a continuous, non-parametric function, the other solving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations -- are trained jointly on NICER X-ray timing posteriors and pulsar mass measurements. The TOV equations enter as a mean-square ODE residual enforced via automatic differentiation at every training step, rooted in the Neural Differential Equation framework. The inferred EOS satisfies nuclear saturation properties, causality, and perturbative QCD bounds simultaneously; $χ$EFT consistency at $1$--$2\rhoz$ emerges without explicit enforcement, providing a non-trivial self-consistency check. Across $N=15$ independent training runs, we find a neutron star maximum mass $M_\mathrm{max}=2.06^{+0.07}_{-0.09}$ and radius and tidal deformability of a 1.4 $M_\odot$ star $R_{1.4}=12.85^{+0.03}_{-0.06}$~km and $Λ_{1.4}=684$, respectively, with 68\% CI, in agreement with recent Bayesian analyses. Most interestingly, the speed of sound exhibits a reproducible softening at $2$--$4\,\rhoz$, consistent with a quark-hadron crossover.

AI.tldr: First application of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to the neutron star equation-of-state inverse problem. Two interacting networks jointly learn the EOS and solve TOV equations, enforcing physics constraints via automatic differentiation. Results match Bayesian analyses and show sound-speed softening consistent with quark-hadron crossover.
AI.motivation: To apply PINNs for the first time to infer the neutron star equation of state from observational data (NICER X-ray timing posteriors and pulsar mass measurements), providing a continuous, non-parametric solution that inherently satisfies physical constraints.
AI.method: Two interacting neural networks: one representing EOS P(ε) as a continuous function, the other solving the TOV equations. TOV equations enforced as mean-square ODE residual via automatic differentiation (Neural ODE framework). Jointly trained on NICER posteriors and pulsar mass measurements across N=15 independent runs.
AI.result: M_max = 2.06^{+0.07}_{-0.09} M⊙, R_1.4 = 12.85^{+0.03}_{-0.06} km, Λ_1.4 = 684 (68% CI). Speed of sound shows reproducible softening at 2-4 ρ₀, consistent with quark-hadron crossover. χEFT consistency at 1-2 ρ₀ emerges without explicit enforcement.
AI.conclusion: PINNs successfully infer the neutron star EOS from observational data, producing results consistent with Bayesian analyses. The method reveals sound-speed softening suggestive of quark-hadron crossover, and satisfies nuclear saturation, causality, and pQCD bounds. Self-consistency with χEFT emerges naturally.

title: Collective Winds of Massive Star Clusters as the Dominant PeVatrons for Galactic Cosmic Rays
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to PRD
summary: The knee feature in the cosmic-ray energy spectrum around 4 PeV is widely believed to have a Galactic origin, but the acceleration mechanism and identification of PeVatrons remain key open questions in high-energy astrophysics. Recent precise measurements by LHAASO reveal that the proton and helium spectra exhibit a common rigidity-dependent spectral break at ~ 3.5 PV, imposing a stringent constraint on source models. In this work, we construct, for the first time, a time-dependent cosmic-ray injection model that incorporates the full evolution of massive stars together with the dynamical development of wind termination shocks. We find that stellar winds of individual massive stars cannot explain the common spectral break observed by LHAASO, as they yield distinct rigidity cutoffs for protons and helium. By contrast, collective winds of massive star clusters naturally reconcile this discrepancy through the mixing effect of stars at different evolutionary stages. We propose a stellar-dominated model in which supernova remnants dominate the GeV-TeV range, individual stellar winds dominate the TeV range, and collective cluster winds dominate the PeV knee region. This model successfully reproduces the rigidity-dependent spectral features of various species near 100 GV and 0.1 PV. It further makes two testable predictions for future observations. Around 0.5 PV, the energy spectra of carbon and oxygen are expected to exhibit hardening similar to that of helium, which can be verified by LHAASO observations. In the multi-TV range, the energy spectrum of magnesium is not expected to show hardening similar to that observed for helium, carbon, and oxygen, which can be tested by DAMPE observations.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a time-dependent cosmic-ray injection model incorporating massive star evolution and wind termination shocks to explain the common rigidity-dependent spectral break at ~3.5 PV observed by LHAASO. It finds individual stellar winds cannot explain the break, but collective winds from star clusters can. A stellar-dominated model is proposed where different sources dominate different energy ranges, reproducing observed spectral features and making testable predictions for carbon/oxygen hardening at ~0.5 PV and magnesium spectral behavior in the multi-TV range.
AI.motivation: The knee feature in the cosmic-ray energy spectrum around 4 PeV is believed to have a Galactic origin, but the acceleration mechanism and identification of PeVatrons remain key open questions. Recent LHAASO measurements of a common rigidity-dependent spectral break at ~3.5 PV impose stringent constraints on source models that need to be explained.
AI.method: A time-dependent cosmic-ray injection model is constructed that incorporates the full evolution of massive stars together with the dynamical development of wind termination shocks. The model compares individual stellar winds versus collective winds from star clusters.
AI.result: Individual stellar winds yield distinct rigidity cutoffs for protons and helium, failing to explain the common break. Collective cluster winds reconcile the discrepancy through mixing effects of stars at different evolutionary stages. The proposed stellar-dominated model (SNR-dominated GeV-TeV, individual stellar winds TeV, collective cluster winds PeV knee) successfully reproduces rigidity-dependent spectral features near 100 GV and 0.1 PV.
AI.conclusion: The model predicts carbon and oxygen hardening similar to helium around 0.5 PV (verifiable by LHAASO), and that magnesium will not show similar hardening in the multi-TV range (testable by DAMPE).

title: Expanding the Population of Short Gamma-Ray Transients with a Coherent Fermi/GBM Search. A 13-year catalog of short GRBs
summary: In this paper, we present an archival search for short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) over 13 years (2013-2025) of Fermi/GBM data using a Poisson matched-filter pipeline that performs a fully coherent analysis across all detectors and energy channels, significantly improving sensitivity relative to the onboard triggering algorithms. A central component of the analysis is the empirical estimation of trigger significance using 'timeslided' data, allowing each candidate to be assigned a probability of astrophysical origin. We also developed a new parameter-estimation framework based on the Poisson matched filter, which uses the global structure of the detected event across spectral, temporal, and spatial parameter spaces. This enables us to systematically classify bursts and distinguish between GRBs, soft gamma repeaters, terrestrial gamma-ray flashes, and solar flares. We identify 568 new GRB candidates with $p_{\text{astro}}\geq0.9$ and thousands of magnetar bursts, significantly expanding the known short-transient population in GBM data. To further strengthen the significance of the GRB candidates, we performed a targeted follow-up search in Swift/BAT rate data. Applying the followup to all of our triggers - including triggers below the detection threshold yielded 1736 temporally coincident events with association probability above $90\%$. The resulting probabilistically ranked catalog substantially expands the population of short GRBs and magnetar flares detected in GBM data and provides a statistically robust framework for multimessenger searches.

AI.tldr: A 13-year (2013–2025) archival search for short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) in Fermi/GBM data using a Poisson matched-filter pipeline with timeslided significance estimation identified 568 new GRB candidates and thousands of magnetar bursts, with 1736 temporally coincident Swift/BAT follow-up events, significantly expanding the known short-transient population and providing a robust framework for multimessenger searches.
AI.motivation: To improve sensitivity for detecting short gamma-ray bursts and other short-duration transients in Fermi/GBM archival data beyond what onboard triggering algorithms can achieve, and to systematically classify burst types (GRBs, SGRs, TGFs, solar flares) with robust statistical significance.
AI.method: A Poisson matched-filter pipeline performing fully coherent analysis across all detectors and energy channels; empirical significance estimation via "timeslided" data; a new parameter-estimation framework using global spectral, temporal, and spatial structure; and targeted follow-up in Swift/BAT rate data for validation.
AI.result: Identified 568 new GRB candidates with p_astro ≥ 0.9, thousands of magnetar bursts, and 1736 temporally coincident Swift/BAT events with >90% association probability.
AI.conclusion: The probabilistically ranked catalog substantially expands the known population of short GRBs and magnetar flares in GBM data and provides a statistically robust framework for multimessenger searches.

title: JWST Predictions for $z > 10$ Galaxies from the Renaissance Simulations -- I: Photometry and Sizes
comment: 26 pages, 20 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome
summary: JWST has enabled new high redshift observations with 14 spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z > 10$ to date, leading to a need for high redshift, high resolution simulations to interpret these observations. We present the physical properties and mock observations of the galaxies in the Renaissance Simulations to add to the growing database of high redshift simulation data to guide and interpret observations. We find that they provide an accurate representation of the formation history of JWST's $z > 10$ discoveries and follow the trends observed in JWST galaxies but extended to lower masses. The stellar masses of the Renaissance galaxies range from $\approx 10^{3}$ to $10^8 M_{\odot}$ and overlap well with the $z > 10$ JWST galaxies with a stellar mass range of about $10^{7}$ to $10^9 M_{\odot}$. The simulated SFRs increase from $10^{-4}$ to $10^1 M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$, overlapping the JWST galaxies' lower SFRs in the range $1 - 20 M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$. These compact galaxies show minimal morphology change as their stellar masses increase with the majority of the half light radii between $1$ and $10$ pc and the majority of the half stellar mass radii around $0.1$ kpc; their Sersic indices vary between $0$ and $4$. The Renaissance galaxies are bluer and generally transition well into the absolute UV magnitudes of the JWST galaxies in the main sequence of galaxies. Overall, our simulations agree well with JWST's discoveries to date, making them a valuable tool in the continued effort to understand the high redshift Universe.

AI.tldr: This paper presents physical properties and mock observations of galaxies from the Renaissance Simulations at z > 10, comparing them with JWST-discovered galaxies. The simulations cover stellar masses ~10^3–10^8 M☉ and SFRs ~10^−4–10^1 M☉/yr, overlapping with observed JWST galaxies (masses ~10^7–10^9 M☉, SFRs ~1–20 M☉/yr). Simulated galaxies are compact (half-light radii 1–10 pc), have Sérsic indices 0–4, and are generally bluer than JWST galaxies. The simulations accurately reproduce JWST's high-redshift discoveries and extend to lower masses, serving as a valuable tool for interpreting observations.
AI.motivation: JWST has revealed 14 spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at z > 10, creating a need for high-resolution simulations at these redshifts to interpret the observational data and understand galaxy formation in the early Universe.
AI.method: The authors use the Renaissance Simulations to generate mock observations and physical properties of high-redshift galaxies, comparing them directly with JWST's z > 10 galaxy sample across stellar mass, star formation rate, morphology (half-light radii, half-stellar mass radii, Sérsic indices), and UV magnitude.
AI.result: Renaissance galaxies span stellar masses 10^3–10^8 M☉ and SFRs 10^−4–10^1 M☉/yr, overlapping with JWST galaxies (10^7–10^9 M☉, 1–20 M☉/yr). They are compact (half-light radii 1–10 pc, half-stellar mass radii ~0.1 kpc) with Sérsic indices 0–4. Simulated galaxies are bluer and extend to lower masses and lower SFRs than current JWST observations, but follow the same trends.
AI.conclusion: The Renaissance Simulations agree well with JWST's z > 10 discoveries, making them a valuable tool for interpreting high-redshift observations and understanding the early Universe.

title: Insights on the Gamma-Ray Bursts variability in their cosmological rest frame
comment: 12 pages, 18 figures Submitted to A&A. Revised version
summary: Gamma-ray bursts temporal profile can be extremely variable, going from a single pulse of a few seconds duration to multiple superimposed pulses occurring over tens or even hundreds of seconds. The variability displayed in the lightcurve of each gamma-ray burst can be the result of the activity taking place in the central engine that generates these violent phenomena, as well as due to magnetic reconnection activities at larger distances. The objective of this work is to find the shortest variability hidden in the lightcurves of the GRBs, with particular focus for the ones with measured redshift, on timescales as short as few milliseconds. This variability will then be related to physical characteristics of the central engine, and evidences of its relation with the spectral parameters of the burst, such as the isotropic energy and peak energy, will be presented. This research is even more relevant in view of the future generation of satellites with improved timing resolution, that will allow us to explore the possible variability in the microsecond region.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the shortest variability timescales in gamma-ray burst (GRB) lightcurves (down to milliseconds), particularly for bursts with measured redshift, aiming to connect this variability to central engine physics and spectral parameters like isotropic energy and peak energy.
AI.motivation: GRB lightcurves are highly variable, and this variability may originate from central engine activity or magnetic reconnection. The goal is to identify the shortest hidden variability timescales to probe central engine characteristics.
AI.method: Analysis of GRB lightcurves focusing on millisecond-scale variability, with special attention to bursts having measured redshift. Variability is related to physical properties of the central engine and spectral parameters (isotropic energy, peak energy).
AI.result: Shortest variability timescales are identified and shown to correlate with physical characteristics of the central engine and with spectral parameters such as isotropic energy and peak energy of the burst.
AI.conclusion: The findings are particularly relevant for future satellites with improved timing resolution, which could explore variability down to microsecond scales, further constraining central engine physics.

title: Euclid preparation. Probing galaxy evolution within cosmic voids in Euclid-like simulations
summary: The evolution of galaxies is profoundly influenced by the environment in which they reside. Cosmic voids serve as pristine laboratories for studying galaxy evolution in the relative absence of the complex physical processes that dominate denser environments. In this study, we investigate galaxy properties and merger histories as a function of environment using the GAlaxy Evolution and Assembly (GAEA) mock-observation lightcone replicating the Euclid Deep Survey as foreseen for the first Euclid data release. The H$α$-selected galaxy sample spans the redshift range $0.4 < z < 1.8$, corresponding to the interval over which H$α$ is accessible to Euclid slitless spectroscopy. We classify galaxies based on their void-centric distance and local density contrast, and compare their stellar mass, specific star formation rate, bulge-to-total stellar mass ratio, and halo mass across different environments. We further analyse the merger histories of these galaxies to study their assembly evolution. We find that galaxies located closer to void centres ($d_{\rm cc} \lesssim 0.7 R_{\rm v}$) are less massive, more actively star-forming, and more disc-dominated than galaxies in denser regions. Merger histories indicate that void galaxies do not experience fewer mergers, but rather that mergers occur later relative to galaxies in high-density regions. These results support a scenario in which the environment regulates the timing and nature of mergers rather than their overall frequency, producing a slower evolutionary path in low-density regions. We conclude by discussing the extent to which these trends are shaped by environmental parametrisation methods and observational selection effects. Our analysis provides a framework for interpreting forthcoming Euclid data and demonstrates Euclid's potential to identify cosmic voids and probe environmental effects on galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: Using GAEA mock-observations replicating the Euclid Deep Survey, this study finds that void galaxies are less massive, more star-forming, more disc-dominated, and experience later mergers compared to galaxies in denser environments, supporting an environment-regulated evolutionary path.
AI.motivation: To understand how cosmic environment (specifically cosmic voids) influences galaxy evolution, using voids as pristine laboratories free from complex processes dominating dense regions.
AI.method: Analyzed Hα-selected galaxy sample (z=0.4-1.8) from GAEA mock-observation lightcone replicating Euclid Deep Survey; classified galaxies by void-centric distance and local density contrast; compared stellar mass, sSFR, bulge-to-total mass ratio, halo mass, and merger histories across environments.
AI.result: Void galaxies (d_cc ≲ 0.7 R_v) are less massive, more star-forming, and more disc-dominated. Merger histories show void galaxies do not have fewer mergers, but mergers occur later than in high-density regions.
AI.conclusion: Environment regulates the timing and nature of mergers rather than their overall frequency, producing slower evolution in low-density regions. Provides framework for interpreting forthcoming Euclid data and demonstrates Euclid's potential for void identification and environmental studies.

title: Simultaneous modeling of FeII emission in the optical and near-infrared in a prototypical Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 galaxy
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ; 21 pages, 15 figures
summary: This work investigates the FeII emission in active galactic nuclei (AGN), combining observational data from optical and near-infrared (NIR) spectra of the prototypical FeII emitter IZw1 with state-of-the-art photoionization modeling. Using updated FeII atomic datasets (Smyth et al. 2019; Tayal & Zatsarinny 2018; Bautista et al. 2015), we explore a wide parameter space to determine the physical conditions of FeII-emitting regions in the broad-line region (BLR). Our results show that optical ($R_{\rm 4570}$) and NIR ($R_{\rm 1μm}$) FeII emission can be simultaneously reproduced under consistent conditions, with the best agreement obtained using the Smyth et al. (2019) dataset, for hydrogen densities of $10^{11.0}$ to $10^{12.0}$ cm$^{-3}$ and near-solar metallicity. We quantify, for the first time, the impact of Lyman-$α$ fluorescence on the physical conditions of FeII emission in both regimes, revealing its dominant role in the NIR and, in contrast, highlighting the stronger influence of collisional processes in the optical. Additionally, for the first time, we compare optical and NIR FeII emission simultaneously with OI and the CaII triplet (CaT), reinforcing their connection to similar spatial regions and physical properties, as well as their usefulness as better proxies for optical FeII. Our findings support the idea of a vertical BLR structure, with NIR FeII and OI originating in less dense regions of the cloud than optical FeII and CaT.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates FeII emission in AGN using observational data from IZw1 and photoionization modeling with updated atomic datasets. It finds that optical and NIR FeII can be simultaneously reproduced under consistent conditions (H densities ~10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³, near-solar metallicity), with Lyman-α fluorescence dominating NIR and collisions dominating optical. It also compares FeII with OI and CaII triplet, supporting a vertical BLR structure.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical conditions of FeII-emitting regions in the BLR of AGN and resolve discrepancies between optical and NIR FeII emission modeling using updated atomic datasets.
AI.method: Combined observational optical/NIR spectra of IZw1 with photoionization modeling using three updated FeII atomic datasets (Smyth et al. 2019; Tayal & Zatsarinny 2018; Bautista et al. 2015), exploring a wide parameter space of density, metallicity, and other physical conditions.
AI.result: Optical (R₄₅₇₀) and NIR (R₁μm) FeII emission are simultaneously reproduced with the Smyth et al. (2019) dataset at H densities 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ and near-solar metallicity. Lyman-α fluorescence dominates NIR FeII, while collisional processes dominate optical FeII. OI and CaT correlate with FeII, supporting a vertical BLR structure where NIR FeII and OI arise in less dense regions than optical FeII and CaT.
AI.conclusion: Updated atomic datasets enable self-consistent modeling of FeII across optical and NIR. The vertical BLR stratification model is supported, with different species tracing different density regimes. OI and CaT serve as useful proxies for optical FeII.

title: Multi-Scale Magnetic Field Observations Reveal how Colliding Flows Trigger Star Formation
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ; 23 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables; includes ancillary movies
summary: Magnetic fields play a crucial yet complex role in star formation, while their connection between large-scale filamentary clouds and small-scale young stellar objects remains poorly understood. We present new continuum polarization observations from the JCMT, ACA, and ALMA that provide continuous magnetic field measurements from approximately 5 pc down to approximately 4000 au, tracing for the first time the evolution of field morphology seamlessly across all key scales within a massive star-forming system. Our polarization maps reveal multiple U-shaped magnetic field structures pointing toward the central protocluster, aligned with accreting filaments from parsec to subparsec scales and converging at the compact center. This morphology suggests an environment of colliding flows that drag magnetic fields and trigger massive protocluster formation. On approximately 4000 au scales, we identify compact U-shaped fields likely guiding the kinematics of streamers accreting onto dense cores. The increasing curvature of these U-shaped patterns is a direct measure of a growing magnetic field tension force, implying a magnetic field strength scaling index of 0.50 +/- 0.10. These results indicate that the field, possibly enhanced by large-scale flow collisions, becomes strong enough to regulate star formation, linking parsec-scale colliding flows, a subparsec hub-filament system, and the triggering of massive star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents multi-scale polarization observations (5 pc to ~4000 au) of a massive star-forming system, revealing U-shaped magnetic fields aligned with accreting filaments and converging at a central protocluster. The increasing curvature indicates a magnetic field strength scaling index of 0.50±0.10, suggesting fields enhanced by colliding flows regulate star formation across scales.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap in understanding how magnetic fields connect large-scale filamentary clouds to small-scale young stellar objects in massive star formation, as this multi-scale relationship remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Continuum polarization observations from JCMT, ACA, and ALMA providing continuous magnetic field measurements from ~5 pc down to ~4000 au, tracing field morphology across all key scales in a massive star-forming system.
AI.result: Discovery of multiple U-shaped magnetic field structures pointing toward the central protocluster, aligned with accreting filaments across scales; identification of compact U-shaped fields at ~4000 au guiding streamer accretion; magnetic field strength scaling index of 0.50±0.10 derived from increasing curvature.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic field, possibly enhanced by large-scale flow collisions, becomes strong enough to regulate star formation, linking parsec-scale colliding flows, subparsec hub-filament systems, and the triggering of massive star formation.

title: The JADES Mass-Metallicity and Fundamental Metallicity Relations at $z\gtrsim2$ Using New High-Redshift Metallicity Calibrations
comment: 24 pages, 10 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present measurements of the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) and fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) at $1.4<z<7.0$ using stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 601 star-forming galaxies from the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES). Using the most up-to-date strong-line metallicity calibrations based on high-redshift galaxies, we derive gas-phase metallicities from composite spectra binned by stellar mass, redshift, and star-forming main sequence (SFMS) offset. We find that the MZR slope evolves weakly from $z\sim0$ out to $z\sim5$, with $γ\sim0.21\pm0.03$, while the normalization decreases smoothly with redshift at a rate of $d\log(\mathrm{O/H})/dz\sim-0.1$ out to $z\sim4$. Beyond $z\gtrsim5$, the low-mass end continues to decline in metallicity while the high-mass end remains broadly consistent with lower-redshift relations, producing a steeper overall MZR. We additionally find evidence for a shallow anti-correlation between deviations from the MZR and SFMS at fixed stellar mass at $z\sim1.4-5$. This anti-correlation, albeit with weaker SFR coupling than observed locally, suggests that an FMR is already beginning to emerge by $z\sim5$. Comparisons with recent observations and cosmological simulations show broad agreement, though no single simulation simultaneously reproduces the observed slopes and normalizations across all redshifts. Our results support a picture in which bursty star formation and strong stellar feedback increasingly shape the regulation of galaxy growth at high redshift, while also highlighting the need for substantially larger spectroscopic samples to robustly constrain the evolution of galaxy scaling relations at high-redshift.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) and fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) at 1.4<z<7.0 using stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 601 star-forming galaxies from JADES. The MZR slope evolves weakly out to z~5 (γ~0.21±0.03), with normalization decreasing at dlog(O/H)/dz~-0.1 out to z~4. Beyond z≳5, the MZR steepens. A shallow anti-correlation between MZR deviations and star-forming main sequence offset suggests an FMR emerging by z~5. Results broadly agree with simulations but highlight the need for larger samples.
AI.motivation: To constrain the evolution of the mass-metallicity relation and fundamental metallicity relation at high redshift (z~1.4-7.0) using JWST/NIRSpec data, and to understand how bursty star formation and stellar feedback regulate galaxy growth in the early universe.
AI.method: Stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 601 star-forming galaxies from JADES were binned by stellar mass, redshift, and star-forming main sequence offset. Gas-phase metallicities were derived using strong-line calibrations based on high-redshift galaxies.
AI.result: The MZR slope evolves weakly from z~0 to z~5 (γ~0.21±0.03), with normalization decreasing at dlog(O/H)/dz~-0.1 out to z~4. At z≳5, the low-mass end declines further while the high-mass end remains consistent with lower redshifts, steepening the MZR. A shallow anti-correlation between MZR deviations and SFMS offset is found at z~1.4-5, indicating an emerging FMR.
AI.conclusion: Bursty star formation and strong stellar feedback increasingly regulate galaxy growth at high redshift. No single simulation simultaneously reproduces all observed slopes and normalizations. Larger spectroscopic samples are needed to robustly constrain high-redshift galaxy scaling relations.

title: Automated void identification by Blendmask: from hierarchical molecular gas to hierarchical voids in NGC 628
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We identify voids in NGC 628 from the JWST MIRI F770W image using a deep_learning method (BlendMask) and refine them by intensity contrast. These voids may be feedback_driven bubbles or dynamically formed structures. Cross_matching with archival star cluster/association catalogs shows that only up to 17.6% of voids are associated with such stellar populations. HST B_band peak_flux distributions of voids with and without these populations overlap substantially, suggesting many related clusters/associations remain unidentified or misclassified. Voids associated with star clusters/associations tend to have lower intensity contrast and larger sizes. An anti_correlation between void size and intensity contrast indicates larger voids have emptier centers, possibly due to stronger feedback. Thus, voids may provide a complementary tracer for identifying stellar populations and constraining their physical properties. To quantify spatial relationships among CO, 21$μ$m, H$_α$ sources, and voids, we construct networks linking each source pair. Among the nine networks, 21$μ$m and H$_α$ sources show the strongest spatial association. Compared to small voids, large voids exhibit progressively increasing separations from CO to 21$μ$m to H$_α$ sources to voids, consistent with an evolutionary sequence in space and time. Smaller voids lie closer to molecular clouds, while larger voids are more displaced. Compared with molecular clouds not associated with voids, those associated with voids are significantly more massive and appear more evolved. Indeed, 68% of molecular clouds associated with voids are also associated with 21$μ$m sources. These results support an evolutionary scenario where some voids originate within molecular clouds, grow through stellar feedback, and gradually detach from their parent clouds.

AI.tldr: The paper uses a deep learning method (BlendMask) to identify voids in NGC 628 from JWST MIRI F770W images, finding that only ~17.6% are associated with known star clusters/associations. Larger voids have emptier centers (anti-correlation between size and intensity contrast). Spatial network analysis reveals an evolutionary sequence from CO → 21μm → Hα → voids, with larger voids progressively more displaced from molecular clouds. Voids associated with molecular clouds tend to be more massive and evolved, supporting an evolutionary scenario where voids originate in molecular clouds, grow via stellar feedback, and detach from parent clouds.
AI.motivation: To identify voids (feedback-driven bubbles or dynamically formed structures) in NGC 628 using JWST data and deep learning, and to understand their relationship with stellar populations and interstellar medium components.
AI.method: Voids identified via BlendMask (deep learning) on JWST MIRI F770W image, refined by intensity contrast. Cross-matched with archival star cluster/association catalogs. Constructed spatial networks linking CO, 21μm, Hα sources, and voids to quantify spatial relationships.
AI.result: Only up to 17.6% of voids associated with known stellar populations. HST B-band peak flux distributions overlap substantially. Voids with clusters/associations have lower intensity contrast and larger sizes. Anti-correlation between void size and intensity contrast. Spatial networks show 21μm and Hα sources have strongest spatial association. Large voids show increasing separations from CO→21μm→Hα→voids. 68% of molecular clouds associated with voids also associated with 21μm sources.
AI.conclusion: Voids serve as complementary tracers for identifying stellar populations and constraining their properties. Results support an evolutionary scenario where voids form in molecular clouds, grow via feedback, and detach from parent clouds.

title: An extended catalogue of Herbig-Haro objects
comment: 64 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We present an extended catalogue of 1193 Herbig-Haro (HH) objects, comprising 477 isolated HH objects and 716 HH knots, compiled through a meticulous review of the literature available through mid-2025. The catalogue provides comprehensive data for each entry, including celestial coordinates, distances, knot separations, exciting sources (with spectral types where available), object characteristics, and bibliographic references. We also perform a preliminary statistical analysis of key parameters such as distance, exciting source properties, morphology, and excitation state. By combining our extended catalogue with the two earlier HH object catalogues published by Hippel et al. in 1988 and Reipurth in 2000, astronomers can access comprehensive information on all known HH objects, thereby facilitating research on star formation and stellar outflows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an extended catalogue of 1,193 Herbig-Haro objects (477 isolated HH objects and 716 HH knots) compiled from literature through mid-2025, with comprehensive data including coordinates, distances, exciting sources, morphology, and references, alongside a preliminary statistical analysis.
AI.motivation: To provide an up-to-date, comprehensive catalogue of known Herbig-Haro objects to facilitate research on star formation and stellar outflows, as previous catalogues (Hippel et al. 1988, Reipurth 2000) are outdated.
AI.method: Meticulous review of literature through mid-2025 to compile 1,193 HH objects; provision of celestial coordinates, distances, knot separations, exciting sources with spectral types, object characteristics, and references; preliminary statistical analysis of distance, exciting source properties, morphology, and excitation state.
AI.result: Extended catalogue of 1,193 HH objects (477 isolated, 716 knots) with comprehensive parameters; statistical trends in distances, source properties, morphology, and excitation states.
AI.conclusion: Combining this extended catalogue with earlier catalogues (Hippel et al. 1988, Reipurth 2000) enables comprehensive access to all known HH objects, aiding future star formation and outflow studies.

title: The Galactic Squeeze: How Aggregate and Highly Dynamical Environments Shape Star Formation in the Local Universe
comment: Abridged Abstract, 21 Pages, 12 Figures, 9 Tables
summary: We investigate how galaxy evolution varies with environment in the nearby Universe by comparing an ``average'' reference volume in the Southern Galactic Pole (SGP) dataset from \citet{VanKempen2024} to the Nexus region, a dynamically assembling superstructure centred on the Abell~4038 galaxy cluster. We quantify environmental effects using the quenched fraction ($f_{\mathrm{Q}}$) and the specific star formation rate ($\mathrm{sSFR}$) for the star-forming population, measured as functions of stellar mass and group-scale halo mass from \citet{VanKempen2026}. We decouple the stellar--halo mass dependence, demonstrating that $f_{\mathrm{Q}}$ increases with stellar mass in both field and group environments, while group galaxies show an additional dependence on halo mass. The Nexus exhibits systematic differences relative to the SGP baseline, consistent with increased heterogeneity in accretion histories and pre-processing within a forming superstructure. For star-forming galaxies, the mean $\log(\mathrm{sSFR})$ declines strongly with stellar mass and shows additional environment-linked suppression in group-scale halos. Within the Nexus, splitting the sample into three projected radial zones around Abell~4038 shows that environmental regulation is not spatially uniform, driven largely by variations in the sampled halo mass function. Finally, a projected phase-space (PPS) analysis of Abell~4038 links quenching to orbital history within the cluster, though this trend is strongly mass-dependent: low-mass galaxies ($\log(M_{\mathrm{stellar}}) < 10$) show no significant change in $f_{\mathrm{Q}}$. These results demonstrate that the drivers of galaxy evolution depend jointly on stellar mass, local group halo mass, and location within the surrounding large-scale structure, motivating future large-scale, multi-wavelength cosmic web surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper compares galaxy evolution in an average field (SGP) versus the dynamically forming Nexus superstructure (centered on Abell~4038), using quenched fraction and sSFR as functions of stellar and halo mass. It finds that quenching depends jointly on stellar mass, group halo mass, and location within large-scale structure, with non-uniform environmental effects across the superstructure and mass-dependent quenching signatures in cluster phase-space.
AI.motivation: To investigate how galaxy evolution varies with environment by comparing an average reference volume to a dynamically assembling superstructure, in order to understand the role of large-scale structure and pre-processing in galaxy quenching.
AI.method: Quantify quenched fraction and sSFR as functions of stellar mass and group-scale halo mass, decouple stellar–halo mass dependence, compare Nexus region to SGP baseline, split Nexus into radial zones around Abell~4038, and perform projected phase-space analysis.
AI.result: Quenched fraction increases with stellar mass in both field and group environments, with additional halo mass dependence for group galaxies. Nexus shows systematic differences from SGP due to heterogeneous accretion histories and pre-processing. sSFR declines with stellar mass and shows environment-linked suppression in groups. Environmental regulation is spatially non-uniform within the Nexus, and phase-space analysis of Abell~4038 reveals mass-dependent quenching linked to orbital history (low-mass galaxies show no significant change).
AI.conclusion: Galaxy evolution drivers depend jointly on stellar mass, local group halo mass, and location within large-scale structure, motivating future multi-wavelength cosmic web surveys.

title: Unveiling the population of massive quenched galaxies at $z\ge2$ in the COLIBRE simulations -- II. The role of AGN feedback and environment on their emergence
comment: Submitted for publication in MNRAS. This work is Part II of a two-paper series (Part I: arXiv:2512.16208). 23 pages (17 of main body and 6 of appendices). Comments welcome
summary: Early ($z \gtrsim 2$) Massive ($M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$), Quenched Galaxies (MQGs) challenge current galaxy formation models. In this series, we study these systems using the new COLIBRE cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. Following the broad agreement between its predictions and observations found in the first paper, this second paper explores the processes driving galaxies to become massive and quenched in COLIBRE, identifying Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) feedback as the primary quenching mechanism in both the thermal (L200m6 simulation) and hybrid (thermal+jet, L200m7h simulation) AGN feedback models implemented. However, the two models behave differently: while the thermal model efficiently quenches massive galaxies at $z>3$, the hybrid model is less effective because black holes (BHs) grow more slowly in the early Universe, and the jet component, which dominates the feedback energy, acts on longer timescales to impact galaxies. Both models predict quasar-like MQGs (AGN with $L_{\rm bol}\gtrsim10^{45}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$), with the most luminous systems associated with more recently quenched galaxies. Compared to star-forming galaxies of similar mass, MQGs host more massive BHs and exhibit higher star formation efficiencies. These differences arise primarily from their environments before quenching, particularly at local ($\rm 0.3\,cMpc$) to intermediate scales ($\rm 1.0\,cMpc$), where overdense regions are associated with enhanced gas inflows, higher BH accretion and, hence, feedback power. We find that about $54\%$ ($20\%$) of the $z=3$ MQGs survive as the main progenitors of $z=0$ galaxies, although up to $56\%$ ($60\%$) experience rejuvenation episodes at $z<3$ in L200m6 (L200m7h). Our results highlight the central role of BH growth, AGN feedback and environment in driving rapid quenching in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes Early Massive Quenched Galaxies (MQGs) at z>2 using COLIBRE simulations, finding that AGN feedback is the primary quenching mechanism, with thermal and hybrid (thermal+jet) models behaving differently in quenching efficiency and timescales. About 54-20% of z=3 MQGs survive to z=0, with significant rejuvenation episodes.
AI.motivation: Early Massive Quenched Galaxies (MQGs) at z≳2 challenge current galaxy formation models. This study aims to understand the physical processes that drive galaxies to become both massive and quenched at high redshift.
AI.method: Analyzed the COLIBRE cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, comparing thermal (L200m6) and hybrid (thermal+jet, L200m7h) AGN feedback models, examining BH growth, feedback mechanisms, environmental conditions, and progenitor tracking.
AI.result: AGN feedback is the primary quenching mechanism in both models. The thermal model quenches efficiently at z>3; the hybrid model is less effective due to slower BH growth and longer jet feedback timescales. About 54% (L200m6) and 20% (L200m7h) of z=3 MQGs survive to z=0, with 56-60% experiencing rejuvenation. MQGs have more massive BHs and higher star formation efficiencies than star-forming galaxies of similar mass.
AI.conclusion: BH growth, AGN feedback (particularly the jet component), and local-to-intermediate scale environmental overdensities are central to driving rapid quenching in the early Universe.

title: Super-Eddington accretion of black holes in early nuclear bursts gives birth to Little Red Dots
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures; submitted to ApJL; comments are welcome
summary: In a recent paper, Chen et al. developed a framework for modeling the seeding and growth of supermassive black holes (BHs) in the context of $Λ$CDM cosmogony. Here, we use a set of physically motivated criteria to select a population of predicted BHs and link them to Little Red Dots (LRDs) discovered by JWST. We show that the LRD population at high redshift ($z$) emerges naturally from a subset of BHs with super-Eddington accretion during nuclear bursts. The model suggests that the observed LRDs are the "tip of the iceberg" of a much larger population of less luminous BHs in the same subset. The model makes specific predictions for the LRD population, such as the mass distributions of their BHs and host galaxies/halos, and the piece-wise redshift evolution of their number density. The cosmological context of the model also allows us to link the observed LRD population to their progenitors (their BH seeds) and lower-$z$ descendant BHs, galaxies and halos. Most LRDs at $z\sim 5$ are seeded at $z \gtrsim 20$ through direct-collapse BHs or pair-instability supernovae from Pop-III stars, and have grown to $M_{\rm BH} \approx 10^5$--$10^7\,{\rm M}_\odot$ through nuclear bursts by their observed redshift. LRDs are predicted to have diverse descendants, ranging from compact dwarf galaxies to brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) at $z=0$. These predictions are consistent with current observations and can be further tested. The success of this model indicates that the results presented here provide a robust foundation for building detailed models of the LRD population.

AI.tldr: This paper uses physically motivated criteria to link supermassive black hole seeding/growth models to JWST-discovered Little Red Dots (LRDs), showing they are super-Eddington accreting BHs representing the "tip of the iceberg" of a larger population, with specific predictions for masses, redshift evolution, progenitors (direct-collapse BHs or Pop-III pair-instability SNe at z≳20), and diverse descendants (from dwarf galaxies to BCGs at z=0).
AI.motivation: To connect physically motivated BH seeding and growth models to the observed Little Red Dot (LRD) population discovered by JWST, and understand their origins, evolution, and relationship to the broader BH population.
AI.method: Applying physically motivated selection criteria to BH populations predicted by the Chen et al. ΛCDM-based framework to identify those corresponding to LRDs, focusing on super-Eddington accretion during nuclear bursts.
AI.result: LRDs emerge naturally as super-Eddington accreting BHs; they represent only the tip of a much larger less-luminous BH population. Model predicts BH/host mass distributions, piece-wise number density evolution, progenitors via direct-collapse or Pop-III pair-instability SNe at z≳20, BH masses of 10⁵–10⁷ M☉ at observed redshift, and diverse descendants from compact dwarf galaxies to BCGs at z=0.
AI.conclusion: The model predictions are consistent with current observations and provide a robust foundation for building detailed LRD population models, with further observational tests possible.

title: MAUVE-MUSE: When Metallicity Follows or Fights Star Formation -- A Mass-Dependent Inversion in Virgo Galaxies
comment: 20 pages, 7 figues, accepted by MNRAS
summary: Although globally-integrated studies often find that, at fixed stellar mass, high star formation rate (SFR) galaxies are relatively metal-poor while lower-SFR systems are more metal-rich, the corresponding coupling between gas-phase metallicity ($Z_{\rm gas}$) and star formation on sub-galactic scales remains poorly constrained. In this study, we analyse 14 Virgo spirals from the MAUVE-MUSE survey to revisit the resolved mass-metallicity relation (rMZR) and its secondary dependence on SFR surface density ($Σ_\mathrm{SFR}$) at $\sim 100$\,pc scales. We construct co-spatial maps of stellar mass surface density ($Σ_*$), $Σ_\mathrm{SFR}$, and oxygen abundance. MAUVE-MUSE galaxies follow a standard rMZR, but when binned by $Σ_*$, we find a mass-dependent inversion in the $Z_\mathrm{gas}$-$Σ_\mathrm{SFR}$ relation using O3N2 calibrations: the standard anti-correlation is confined to low-$Σ_*$ bins, while high-$Σ_*$ regions show a positive correlation, inverting at $\log_{10}(Σ_*/M_\odot\,\mathrm{kpc}^{-2})\simeq 7.5$-8.0. Correlated and anti-correlated \ion{H}{ii} regions coexist within the same discs; the mass dependence emerges only when grouping spaxels by $Σ_*$. We develop a spatially resolved gas-regulator model showing this $Z_\mathrm{gas}$-$Σ_\mathrm{SFR}$ (anti-)correlation arises from competition between star-formation-driven and gas-supply-driven variability. This framework naturally extrapolates to the integrated scenario, providing a unified explanation for resolved and global relations. However, the presence and strength of the $Z_\mathrm{gas}$-$Σ_\mathrm{SFR}$ (anti-)correlation depend strongly on the metallicity indicator used, highlighting the challenge of disentangling physical secondary trends within metallicity scaling relations.

AI.tldr: Using 14 Virgo spirals from MAUVE-MUSE at ~100 pc scales, the study finds a mass-dependent inversion in the resolved $Z_{\rm gas}$-$\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ relation: low-$\Sigma_*$ regions show anti-correlation (metal-poor high-SFR), high-$\Sigma_*$ regions show positive correlation. A spatially-resolved gas-regulator model explains this as competition between star-formation-driven outflows and gas-supply-driven enrichment. The effect is metallicity-calibration dependent.
AI.motivation: While the global mass-metallicity relation's secondary SFR dependence is well-known at integrated scales, the corresponding resolved (sub-galactic, ~100 pc) coupling between gas-phase metallicity and star formation remains poorly constrained.
AI.method: Analyzed 14 Virgo cluster spirals from MAUVE-MUSE survey; constructed co-spatial maps of $\Sigma_*$, $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$, and oxygen abundance at ~100 pc scales; developed a spatially-resolved gas-regulator model.
AI.result: The $Z_{\rm gas}$-$\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ relation inverts at $\log_{10}(\Sigma_*/M_\odot\,{\rm kpc}^{-2})\simeq 7.5$–8.0: low-$\Sigma_*$ bins show the standard anti-correlation, high-$\Sigma_*$ bins show a positive correlation. Both correlated and anti-correlated H II regions coexist within the same disc. The signal is strongly dependent on the metallicity calibration (e.g., O3N2).
AI.conclusion: The resolved $Z_{\rm gas}$-$\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ (anti-)correlation arises from competition between star-formation-driven outflow (dilution) and gas-supply-driven enrichment, unifying resolved and global relations. However, the strong calibration dependence cautions against over-interpreting secondary trends in metallicity scaling relations.

title: Enhancing Galaxy Classification with U-Net Variational Autoencoders. III. Disk-like Galaxy Identification in JWST Samples of up to redshift 4
summary: In this third study of the series, we extend our U-Net Variational Autoencoder-based galaxy classification framework to a significantly larger JWST sample spanning the redshift range $0.5 < z < 4$. Focusing on massive systems with stellar masses exceeding $10^{10}\,M_\odot$, we analyze 1,380 galaxies that satisfy these criteria and apply our previously developed denoising and classification pipeline to identify disk-like morphologies across cosmic time. Within this population, our classifier detects 382 disk-like galaxies, with a subset showing uncertain features consistent with the expected performance limits of current deep-learning models. This expanded dataset allows us to examine the distribution of disk-like systems in a statistically meaningful high-redshift regime, including epochs where well-ordered disks are traditionally expected to be rare. The results demonstrate that disk-like structures persist across a broad range of redshifts and stellar masses, suggesting that massive disks may be more common in the early universe than previously assumed. These findings emphasize the value of combining advanced denoising techniques with machine-learning-based morphological analysis for characterizing galaxy populations in large JWST surveys.

AI.tldr: This study extends a U-Net Variational Autoencoder galaxy classification framework to 1,380 massive JWST galaxies (z=0.5–4, M>10¹⁰ M☉), identifying 382 disk-like systems. Results show disk-like structures persist across a broad redshift range, suggesting massive disks are more common in the early universe than previously assumed.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether well-ordered disk-like galaxies exist at high redshifts where they are traditionally expected to be rare, using a larger and statistically meaningful JWST sample.
AI.method: Applied a U-Net Variational Autoencoder-based denoising and classification pipeline to 1,380 massive galaxies (M>10¹⁰ M☉) from JWST data spanning 0.5<z<4.
AI.result: Detected 382 disk-like galaxies (with some uncertain subset at model performance limits); disk-like structures persist across broad redshift and stellar mass ranges.
AI.conclusion: Massive disk galaxies may be more common in the early universe than previously assumed, highlighting the value of combining advanced denoising with machine-learning morphological analysis for large JWST surveys.

title: Dynamics of tidal tails of open clusters: I. effects of bar, spiral arms and giant molecular clouds
summary: Open clusters gradually dissolve, and their stars disperse into the Galactic field. Lost stars form tidal tails-elongated streams that trace the cluster orbit ahead of and behind its core. From the shape and orientation of the tidal tails, it is possible to infer the shape of the gravitational potential governing the cluster's motion. The orbits of open clusters, including those in the Solar neighbourhood, are sensitive to the gravitational potential of the inner Galaxy, which is dominated by the Galactic bar. Using n-body simulations of synthetic and real open clusters, we investigate how sensitive the shapes and orientations of tidal tails are to variations of the gravitational potential of the Milky Way. We consider the effects of the bar as well as spiral arms, giant molecular clouds (GMCs) and satellite galaxies. We analyse the stellar distributions within tidal tails using statistical metrics that quantify the differences between tail morphologies. Such non-parametric approach enables us to efficiently explore tidal tails across a large parameter space of gravitational potential models. We find that the Galactic bar-particularly its pattern speed-has a strong influence on the orbits of open clusters and the shape of their tails. Spiral arms have a limited effect, and satellite galaxies do not disturb the tidal tails of nearby open clusters. Perturbations by GMCs affect most clusters, with distortions stronger than those by the bar observed in old and in-plane clusters. We identify nearby open clusters that are most sensitive to the pattern speed of the bar. By observing the tidal tails of a handful of well-selected nearby clusters, we should be able to measure the pattern speed of the bar with a precision in the order of $1\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,kpc^{-1}}$ independently from length and orientation of the bar. We will present the observability of tidal tails in paper II.

AI.tldr: Using N-body simulations, this study investigates how tidal tails of open clusters are shaped by the Milky Way's gravitational potential, finding the Galactic bar's pattern speed has the strongest influence, and that observing tidal tails of nearby clusters could measure the bar's pattern speed to ~1 km/s/kpc precision.
AI.motivation: To understand how the gravitational potential of the Milky Way—particularly the Galactic bar—affects the shapes and orientations of tidal tails from dissolving open clusters, and to explore whether these tails can be used as probes of the bar's properties.
AI.method: N-body simulations of synthetic and real open clusters were run under varying gravitational potential models including the Galactic bar, spiral arms, giant molecular clouds (GMCs), and satellite galaxies. Statistical non-parametric metrics were used to quantify differences in tidal tail morphologies across a large parameter space.
AI.result: The Galactic bar's pattern speed strongly influences cluster orbits and tail shapes; spiral arms have limited effect; satellites do not disturb nearby cluster tails; GMCs cause distortions stronger than the bar in old, in-plane clusters. Nearby clusters most sensitive to bar pattern speed were identified.
AI.conclusion: Observing tidal tails of a handful of well-selected nearby open clusters could measure the bar's pattern speed with ~1 km/s/kpc precision, independently of the bar's length and orientation. Observability will be addressed in a follow-up paper.

title: Reconciling the Fundamental Plane of Early-Type Galaxies with hydrodynamical simulations: The case of IllustrisTNG100-1
comment: Manuscript submitted to MNRAS
summary: The Fundamental Plane (FP) of Early-Type Galaxies (ETGs) encapsulates a tight correlation among their structural and dynamical properties and provides an important benchmark for galaxy formation models. However, cosmological hydrodynamical simulations have historically struggled to reproduce the observed FP tilt, with discrepancies often attributed to to flawed feedback physics or insufficient resolution. Using the IllustrisTNG100-1 simulation, we show that adopting observationally motivated measurements, including Sérsic-derived photometric parameters and dynamically inferred velocity dispersions designed to minimise softening-length effects, substantially reduces the discrepancy between simulated and observed FPs. We further explore the impact of non-universal, mass-dependent Initial Mass Function (IMF) variations through forward modelling of their effects on galaxy structural and dynamical quantities. In particular, bottom-heavy IMF variations produce FP coefficients fully consistent with observational constraints for both direct and orthogonal fits. Our results suggest that a significant fraction of the long-standing FP tension arises from how galaxy observables are extracted and interpreted in simulations, although residual discrepancies may still reflect limitations in the underlying baryonic physics. These findings highlight the importance of observational realism and IMF variations for interpreting galaxy scaling relations and for improving the predictive power of hydrodynamical simulations of ETG formation.

AI.tldr: Using IllustrisTNG100-1 simulations with observationally motivated measurements (Sérsic photometry, dynamically inferred velocity dispersions) and mass-dependent IMF variations, the long-standing tension between simulated and observed Fundamental Plane of early-type galaxies is substantially reduced, indicating that discrepancies largely stem from how observables are extracted.
AI.motivation: Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations have historically struggled to reproduce the observed FP tilt of ETGs, with discrepancies often attributed to flawed feedback physics or insufficient resolution.
AI.method: Used IllustrisTNG100-1 simulation; adopted Sérsic-derived photometric parameters and dynamically inferred velocity dispersions designed to minimise softening-length effects; forward modelled non-universal, mass-dependent IMF variations.
AI.result: Observationally motivated measurements substantially reduce FP discrepancy; bottom-heavy IMF variations produce FP coefficients fully consistent with observational constraints for both direct and orthogonal fits.
AI.conclusion: A significant fraction of the FP tension arises from how galaxy observables are extracted and interpreted in simulations; observational realism and IMF variations are important for interpreting scaling relations and improving predictive power of hydrodynamical simulations.
